column4: Garment (the clothes, measured flat) or body (the person). Pick one and say it in the chart title.
column12: Garment numbers are easiest for small shops and resale. Buyers can compare them with clothes they already own.

column4: List every size you sell, smallest first. Leave a size column empty if you do not sell it.
column12: Use the same size names as your Shopify variants, so buyers see the same words in both places.

column4: Show cm and inches. Type cm only: the inches rows fill themselves.
column12: Many buyers in the UK and US think in inches. Most of Europe uses cm.

column4: Lay it flat and buttoned. Measure straight across, 2.5 cm (1 inch) below the armholes, from side seam to side seam.
column12: This is the number buyers compare most. Measure 2 items of the same size if you can.

column4: Fills itself from the cm row above. Do not type here.

column4: Pit to pit x 2. This row fills itself.

column4: Say how it fits in a few words, and what to do if they like it closer or looser.
column11: Relaxed fit. For a closer fit, take one size down.
column12: Use the same fit words on every product: slim, regular, relaxed or oversized.

column4: Say the fabric and if it stretches.
column12: No stretch means the numbers in the chart are the most it will give.

column4: Tell buyers which way to go.
column11: Between two sizes? Take the larger one for a relaxed look, the smaller one for a neater fit.
column12: One short sentence stops many "which size?" messages.

column4: Tell buyers how to check at home.
column11: Lay a shirt you love flat, measure it the same way, and pick the size with the closest numbers.
column12: This works for garment charts. It is the fastest way for a buyer to check.

column12: Only add this if it is true for your photos.

column4: Say the numbers are measured by hand.

column12: Only write a number you have checked on your own items.
